content.p: When Serbia and Montenegro drove Ottoman forces out of Kosovo, western Macedonia and northern Albania in the autumn of 1912, they took over land whose countryside, in the words of the Frankfurter Zeitung, was mostly Albanian. Journalists, consuls, a Serbian socialist and an international commission all reported that Albanian civilians were killed in large numbers, that villages were burned, and that thousands fled. The exact number of dead has never been settled.

The record is uneven. Some accounts are first-hand and some are second-hand letters. Others come from newspapers, political movements or historians writing decades later with a stake in the answer. What follows keeps track of who said what, because the toll, the cause and even the right name for these events are still argued over.

The First Balkan War began on 8 October 1912, after Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece had agreed between them to invade Ottoman territory. The historian Justin McCarthy writes that in Ottoman Europe 51 per cent of the population was Muslim, mainly Albanians in the west and Turks in the east, and that the invading states, whose own peoples were a minority, saw eviction and death of the Muslims as the solution. His summary says the speed of the conquest made things worse for civilians, who stayed in their villages waiting for the fighting to end and then fled when irregular bands arrived.

British consuls quoted by McCarthy describe what that looked like further east and south. The consul at Monastir wrote that about 80 per cent of the villages inhabited only by Muslims in that district had been sacked, and added that irregular troops and marauders from nearby Christian villages were probably mainly responsible. Albanians were caught up in the same pattern as Turks.
content.h2: Skopje and the railway to Kosovo, autumn 1912
content.p: Leon Trotsky, then a war correspondent for the Kiev newspaper Kievskaya Misl, set down an account in the autumn of 1912 that he introduced as the words of a Serbian acquaintance, written down almost word for word. The man described going to Skopje a few days after the battle of Kumanovo. Beyond the old Serbian frontier he saw whole Albanian villages burning in the dusk along the railway line. In Skopje, which he put at 60,000 inhabitants, half of them Albanians and Turks, irregular fighters broke into Albanian and Turkish homes at night, and residents found headless bodies piled under the main bridge over the Vardar. Some said local Albanians had been killed there; others said the bodies had been carried down the river. Either way, the account says, the dead had not fallen in battle.

The same account reports soldiers talking openly. A corporal stationed near Ferizović (Ferizaj), the Albanian centre of what the Serbs called Old Serbia, told the narrator, "We are roasting chickens and slaughtering Albanians." He described driving the women out of a prosperous house, killing the men in front of them and setting the village on fire. A cavalryman boasted of killing many Albanians. Serbian peasants who had walked in from Serbia to Kosovo Polje were looking to buy horses and oxen that soldiers fetched from Albanian villages. The corporal also insisted that the regular army killed nobody under twelve and that the irregulars might be different. The report is one man's testimony, passed through a journalist, and it names no victims.

By March 1913 the reports had become a public quarrel. On 14 March the Frankfurter Zeitung ran a front-page editorial after its Skopje correspondent reported that 300 Albanians had been shot by the Serbs without trial. It said the report would be denied, as earlier ones had been, and it rejected the argument that irregulars out of the army's control were to blame. Even where irregulars did the killing, it wrote, it happened with the tacit permission and will of the Serbian authorities.

The paper claimed that the Serbian authorities had said openly at the start of the war that they would exterminate the Albanians. It also said the sources were not Turkish and not Austrian or German but representatives of the Triple Entente, especially English reporters, and that consular reports of most European countries confirmed events. It allowed that soldiers might in some cases have answered shots fired from villages. In its view nothing justified razing hundreds of villages and killing tens of thousands of men, women and children. It added a new report that 300 tribesmen of Luma, caught unarmed, had been shot in Prizren. The editorial is a newspaper's charge, based on correspondents it did not name. The figure of tens of thousands is its own estimate.

A Catholic voice from the same region also reached the outside world. Fintan O'Toole later quoted a letter that Archbishop Lazar Mejda of Skopje wrote to the Pope about Prizren, saying that men were taken from Albanian houses and shot at once and that the number killed in a few days reached 400. According to O'Toole, who was drawing on Noel Malcolm's book Kosovo: A Short History, Mejda estimated that 25,000 Albanians had been massacred in Kosovo by that point. O'Toole's article is a newspaper column from 1999, written to argue a point about the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, and its second-hand figures should be read that way.
content.h2: Luma and Dibra, September and October 1913
content.p: According to the historian Fitim Rifati, Albanian armed groups attacked Serbian forces near the Luma border in the second half of September 1913. He says they pushed in three directions, towards Debar, Ohrid and Prizren, and that the uprising spread across nearly all of Kosovo. Rifati writes that Serbia committed between 20,000 and 50,000 soldiers to suppress it, citing newspapers of the time. He argues that the revolt served the Kingdom of Serbia as a pretext to take back territory in order to widen the strategic border set by the Conference of Ambassadors in London. His article rests heavily on Albanian-language sources and on Serbian and Yugoslav works, and it presents the Albanian side.

The Carnegie commission's report, published in 1914, quotes a letter from a Serbian soldier that appeared in the socialist paper Radnitchke Novine on 9 October (22 October, new style) 1913. "Liouma (an Albanian region along the river of the same name), no longer exists," the soldier wrote. "There is nothing but corpses, dust and ashes. There are villages of 100, 150, 200 houses, where there is no longer a single man, literally not one. We collect them in bodies of forty to fifty, and then we pierce them with our bayonets to the last man." The commissioners wrote that the expedition was known to have been sent to put down an Albanian revolt. They noted that the Serbian side blamed the revolt on agitation from autonomous Albania and on Bulgarian conspiracy. They added that these were probable causes, but that they did not rule out a third, the state of mind of the Albanian population under Serbian rule.

Dimitrije Tucovic, a socialist leader mobilized in 1912, wrote about the same repression in Serbia and Albania. In his Serbian text, as translated here, the Albanian villages were turned into ruins, and he called them "barbaric crematoria" in which hundreds of living women and children burned. He wrote that the government announced the Albanians would be "exemplarily punished" and that the bourgeois press demanded extermination without mercy. He also noted that the insurgents had disarmed and released captured Serbian officers and soldiers. Tucovic was killed at the battle of the Kolubara in November 1914.

The commission also set down an account from Dibra that it could not check. A letter from Elbasan, published in a Bulgarian paper, said that Serbian troops had taken cattle from the Malesia of Dibra in September 1913 and that herdsmen who resisted were killed. It said 48 notables arrested in Dibra town were killed, and that in the village of Sulp 73 Albanians died. The commissioners said they could not verify it but saw no reason to doubt it in view of everything they had seen and heard. Albanians then rose up, the letter says, and drove the Serbian officials and soldiers out of the town.

The Carnegie Endowment's Division of Intercourse and Education set up the commission in July 1913, with Baron d'Estournelles de Constant as president. The other members included Josef Redlich, Justin Godart, Walther Schucking, Francis W. Hirst, H. N. Brailsford and Samuel T. Dutton. They travelled in the Balkans in August and September 1913, and the historian Stefan Troebst notes that the report appeared only after a long delay, its effect largely lost to the July crisis and then the First World War. Troebst says the commission's brief was to investigate massacres and atrocities by combatants against civilians and to identify the guilty.

The report quotes a petition from Albanian representatives, written in September 1913, that the Serbian and Montenegrin regular troops did everything from the first day. It then describes the pattern in its own words: houses and whole villages reduced to ashes, unarmed and innocent people massacred en masse, "incredible acts of violence, pillage and brutality of every kind", all with a view to "the entire transformation of the ethnic character of regions inhabited exclusively by Albanians." The commission was careful about intent. "Orders of extermination" were not given to the Slav armies, it wrote, and orders to the contrary were given. But it added that private conversations constantly showed the same idea.
content.h2: Plav and Gusinje, and the south
content.p: Reports of killing came from Montenegro's new territory too. In March 2013, on the centenary, Muslims in Plav held a mass prayer. Bosniak organisations claim that more than 1,800 Muslims from Plav and Gusinje were killed and more than 12,000 forcibly converted to Christianity in 1912 and 1913. The historian Serbo Rastoder told the Montenegrin paper Vijesti that documents and research show the killings and forced conversions happened, but that the public remains unaware of it. The head of Montenegro's Islamic community said the argument that the central government did not control the newly acquired territory cannot justify a massive crime. Because the 1,800 figure comes from advocacy groups, it is given as their claim.

Greek forces were accused of similar acts in southern Albania in 1914. Christo Dako, an Albanian journalist and activist from Korça, sent a list of burned villages to the British campaigner Aubrey Herbert. It records, for example, that Qinam lost all but 8 of its 55 houses on 1 May. It says that at Kodra, near Tepeleni, villagers were gathered in the Orthodox church and that 230 of them were shot down. Dako cited a Dutch officer, General De Veer, as having seen the scene and photographed it. Dako was an interested party, and these figures come from his report alone.

There is no agreed figure. Rifati cites the Serbian Social Democrat Kosta Novakovic, who put the number of Albanians killed by Serbian and Montenegrin forces from October 1912 to the end of 1913 at more than 120,000, with more than 50,000 forcibly expelled. The historian Muhamed Mufaku notes that the Arab press reported a claim, taken from the Daily Chronicle on 1 December 1912, that Serbian forces killed 5,000 Albanians near Pristina, and he says families fled to Istanbul and as far as Damascus. At village level, Rifati cites one source for the claim that in the Astrazub district about 300 Albanians were killed and 1,029 of 1,380 houses burned in 1913.

McCarthy's estimate of 632,000 Muslim dead covers all of Ottoman Europe, not Albanians alone. It is derived by subtracting survivors from the pre-war population, and he says nobody counted the dead in Albania.
